Not secret · compiled entirely from public records · board of trustees minutes 1997–2026 · OpenAlex · no individual outcome is predicted here
A briefing on the publication record at the moment of decision

Dr. Skylar-Scott

or: How I learned to stop worrying and love the clock

Between 1997-04 and 2026-06, Stanford’s Board of Trustees minuted 20707 appointment actions on 2244 tenure-line faculty. This report reconstructs what each assistant professor’s publication record looked like at matched points on the tenure clock — three and four years in — and asks which measurable things separated the people who were later promoted from the people who left. It is named for one clock among the 5 in Bioengineering that are still running, because the honest answer to “what happens to any one person” is the subject of the final chapter.

129 board reports20707 minuted entries656 tenured · 276 left · 147 undecidedtests Mann–Whitney / Fisher, BH-corrected
I

The War Room

Gentlemen, you can’t fight in here. This is where the data lives.

The population is every assistant professor whose appointment the minutes actually record — the clock start is observed, not inferred. “Tenured” means a later promotion to Associate Professor on the university line appears in the minutes; “left” means the last term ran out and the person next appears somewhere else; “undecided” means the clock is still running, and those records are shown but never scored. Every publication count is point-in-time: work published by 31 December of the anchor year, cited by work published by the same date, on the Stanford clock only.

A clock that runs past year nine ends in tenure 27% of the time and in departure 45%; inside the normal seven years the same numbers are 51% and 15%. The machine is not subtle, but it is slow — and 109 of the 131 long clocks carry at least one data disqualifier, so the sharpest-looking cut is also the least clean. Sources: results/summary.txt, results/rank_year.txt.
II

Wing Attack Plan R — the rate

The volume of publication, held against every other measure, is the order that stands.

At a matched point on the clock, the single strongest separator in the entire battery is how much a person publishes. At year four the median later-tenured record is running 3.6 papers per clock year against 1.4 for the group that left (AUC 0.705, p 3×10-18); the recent-output version — publications in the last three years — tests the same (AUC 0.705). Citations, h-index and every impact measure trail it, and in a joint model — chapter V — they collapse entirely once volume is held.

Volume or pace? At a matched anchor, cumulative volume and publications-per-year are one number; the real question is cumulative volume against the current pace (last three years), and they only decorrelate as the clock runs (r 0.95 at year 4, 0.88 at year 8). Entered jointly: at year four the current pace carries the signal (OR 14.9, p 0.005; volume adds nothing); by year eight it flips — the accumulated body of work wins (OR 15.9, p 0.02) and current pace adds nothing. Early clock, you are your trajectory; late clock, you are your pile. Collinearity widens every interval — read the flip, not the point estimates.

III

The Big Board — flagships

Mr. President, we cannot allow a Nature-paper gap.

A Cell, Nature or Science paper on the clock is rarer than the folklore implies — the median record in both arms has none. But the share is lopsided: 27% of the later-tenured had at least one at year four against 7% of the leavers (p 2×10-10), and in the joint model a first CNS paper carries an odds ratio of 5.7 with volume held. It is a threshold, not a dose: the promotion rate climbs to the first paper and goes flat — 68% with none, 87% with exactly one, 97% with two, and no meaningful gain after. Cut strictly to papers where the person carries the publisher’s corresponding-author flag — no last-author or sole-author fallback — the split is 15% against 3% (p 3×10-7), through a flag that exists on only a quarter of papers.

Threshold, not dose

Year 4. CNS = the three titles exactly; family adds the Nature/Cell/Science sister journals. Two senior-authorship cuts: “led” = last author, flagged corresponding, or sole author, restricted to lab-science departments where position carries seniority; “corresponding” = the publisher’s flag alone, tested in every department because the flag, unlike author order, is not a field convention. The flag is a floor: measured on this corpus it exists on 25% of on-clock papers, 36% of CNS papers (162 of 445).

Publishing in your department’s field

Does the machine care whether you publish where your department publishes? Every work carries an OpenAlex field; a department’s profile is the field distribution of every other cohort member’s on-clock work (leave-one-out), and a person’s alignment is the overlap of their own distribution with it (1 = publishes exactly like the department).

The answer is no — a rare, useful null. Pooled overlap runs 0.56 v 0.53 and misses correction; the blunter “share in the department’s biggest field” separates nothing anywhere; and Engineering runs backwards — its leavers were the more departmentally aligned arm. Only Medicine leans toward rewarding the home field (AUC 0.659, q 0.077). Publishing outside your department’s field is not, in this corpus, a measurable tenure risk — the currency chapters (rate, flagships, funding) do not care where you spend it. And the null holds at every milestone: overlap AUC 0.537 / 0.545 / 0.551 across years 4, 6 and 8, none surviving correction.

IV

The Point of No Return

Past this point, today’s citation counts do not approximate the answer. They invert it.

Every number on this page is a statement about a moment. Persi Diaconis’s pre-1996 papers carry 17,709 citations today; on 31 December 1995 they carried 2,014. Read today’s counts back onto old cases and the oldest cohorts look strongest precisely because they have had the longest to accumulate — the error grows with exactly the thing being studied. OpenAlex’s own per-year counts reach back only to 2012, earlier than half the cases here, so citations were rebuilt from the citing side: every work citing W and published by 31 December of year Y, verified exact against the API’s own totals, ten of ten. The gap between citations and citations_now in the source tables is the size of the error this page exists to avoid. Source: src/SNAPSHOT_README.md.

V

Survival Kit Contents

One hundred dollars in rubles, one hundred dollars in gold, nine packs of chewing gum, one acknowledged federal grant.

Grant success itself is not in the minutes, but the acknowledgements sections of the papers are a proxy the record does carry: OpenAlex preserves each paper’s deposited funding lines. Coverage is the caveat — publishers barely deposited any before 2010, and even in 2015–19 only about 30% of this corpus’s papers carry a line — so the comparison is run both pooled and restricted to the era where the metadata exists. It separates the arms either way: at year four, 63% of the later-tenured had at least one acknowledged grant against 35% of the leavers, and an NIH line specifically splits 41% against 23%.

Acknowledged-funder breadth and as-PI federal money at years 4, 6 and 8, undecided-at-that-year arms.

Acknowledgements are the money visible on papers. The registers answer the sharper question — who held federal money as PI. Every Stanford project in NIH RePORTER (FY1985 on) and every Stanford NSF award was pulled and matched to the cohort by strict name rules: a grant two people could claim is dropped, and a grant that predates the person’s observed arrival is a namesake’s and is excluded. A second, national name-based pass then catches what the Stanford filter cannot see — VA-administered awards, the K99 phase held at a postdoc institution, transfers — admitting a non-Stanford award only when it is acknowledged on the person’s own papers or its institution appears in their OpenAlex affiliation history with overlapping years (fresh awards have no papers yet to acknowledge them, so the affiliation gate covers what the acknowledgement gate cannot). 679 cross-institution awards entered that way, led by the Palo Alto VA. By clock year four, 57% of the later-tenured held at least one NIH or NSF award as PI against 30% of the leavers (p 9×10-14); inside Engineering the same split is 71% against 44%. The record also starts earlier: the promoted began publishing a median of 8 years before the clock, the leavers 6 (q 0.001) — though the gap lives between schools, not within them: inside Engineering and Medicine the two arms start their records at the same time.

Only NIGMS and NINDS survive correction pooled, and inside Medicine no single institute does — holding any NIH award is the signal, not which one. Engineering cannot support this layer at all: its sixteen NIH PIs spread across every institute, because Engineering’s federal life runs through NSF — 64% of its promoted held an NSF award as PI (largely CISE and engineering-directorate programs: Algorithmic Foundations, Robust Intelligence, cyber-physical systems, photonics), and an NSF CAREER award splits 13% against 7% pooled (q 0.03).

The horse race — what survives when entered jointly

One number to rule them all — the principal components

Twelve metrics — the ten record measures plus acknowledged-funder breadth and federal dollars held as PI — each first ranked within its own school-and-era cell, decomposed. PC1 is the general size of the enterprise (62% of variance; publications, citations, venues and the funding columns all loading the same direction) and tests at AUC 0.632 — worse than raw volume’s 0.705, because averaging the strong signal with the weak ones dilutes it. PC2, the shape axis — many recent papers versus a funded one-big-paper profile — predicts nothing (p 0.72). PC3, which sets as-PI dollars and funder breadth against citation depth, carries a residual whisper (AUC 0.561, p 0.01). The committee’s number, if it has one, is still the publication count.

The same decomposition at years 6 and 8

PCA refit on the undecided-at-that-year arms. The anatomy is frozen: at every milestone the same three axes emerge with the same loadings and the same shares of variance. What changes is which axis predicts — the funded-flagship shape (PC3) carries its whisper early and is gone by year eight; the size axis (PC1) only strengthens, peaking exactly where the milestone model says volume takes over. (The pre-tenure anchor is not a valid comparison point here: it exists only for the promoted, and measuring each group at its own endpoint compares different amounts of elapsed career — the inversion this pipeline exists to avoid.) The big-moment model

“A big moment” is made measurable as any of three owned, registry-visible events by year four: a flagship paper the person led, a led paper at the top of its own cell’s citation distribution, or a major award as PI. The model asks what each adds once the size of the pile is held.

A led flagship carries the largest independent odds on the page (OR 4.7) — as heavy as volume itself — and a major award adds real, separate odds (OR 2.6). The citation peak of your best own paper adds nothing once those are counted (OR 0.68, p 0.28) — impact is absorbed; the visible boxes are not. As a single composite: having any big moment carries OR 2.8 with volume held, and lifts the model’s AUC from 0.628 to 0.697 (in-sample, n=753). The honest counterweight: 56% of the later-tenured had no big moment by year four either — the box helps, and most promoted cases never checked it this early.

The same model at each milestone

Refit on the undecided-at-that-year arms. The terms take turns: at year four all three carry odds; by year six the award box has stopped discriminating among the survivors; by year eight only the accumulated volume speaks — and the base rates halve, because a clock still running at year eight is already mostly bad news. The last column is the observed promotion rate from the worst cell (bottom-half volume, no big moment) to the best.

VI

The Mineshaft Gap — school by school

Mr. President, we must not allow the field mix to explain the finding.

Field mix is the standing objection to every pooled number on this page — Medicine publishes more of everything than History, so a pooled test partly measures which schools tenure more people. The answer is to run the whole battery again inside each school. It survives everywhere the cells are big enough to test, and each school separates on its own axis: Engineering on sheer rate (median 8 v 3.8 papers a year, AUC 0.726) and funder breadth; Medicine on recent output, papers led, and funding portfolio — its median leaver still acknowledges 5 distinct funders against the promoted group’s 10; H&S on flagships, where a CNS paper splits 22% against 3% and a corresponding-author one 35 of 248 promoted against 1 of 101 leavers. And GSB separates on nothing: 15 tests, none significant, the closest again the rate (AUC 0.64, q 0.06) — consistent with a school whose departures read as recruitment, and the only school where the leavers outnumber the stayed-and-tenured at year four (n=49 v 40). 57 of 138 school-level tests survive their own BH family.

VII

The Case of M. Skylar-Scott — and the Bioengineering board

Seventeen clocks, one department. Eleven rang tenure, one ran out, five are still ticking.

Bioengineering has had seventeen assistant-clock hires in the archive — too few for department-level statistics, which is exactly why they are shown as people rather than percentages. Mark Skylar-Scott’s clock started July 2020 and currently runs to June 2028; at year four his lab was publishing 2.8 papers a year with 351 point-in-time citations. Po-ssu Huang’s clock started October 2016 and is in its tenth year without a minuted promotion; his latest reappointment is an eleven-month term ending February 2027 — in the corpus, terms shaped like that are how a clock winds down. Paul Nuyujukian’s clock started September 2016 and his terms now run to September 2026. The minutes record no denial for anyone — denials are never minuted; people simply stop being reappointed — so all three stand as undecided here, and this page predicts nothing about any of them.

A row exists at year N only while that case was still open — resolved cases stop being measured, so the table thins as the clock runs (16 → 11 → 4). as corr. counts only papers where the person carries the publisher’s corresponding-author flag — the strictest “their papers” cut, and a floor: the flag is deposited on only about a quarter of papers corpus-wide (though more reliably in recent years and in this department’s venues). Raw pubs count everything including middle-author collaborations — Skylar-Scott’s 18 at year six are 7 as corresponding, 9 in the middle of someone else’s list. ⚠ Two records carry OpenAlex merged-identity contamination; Po-ssu Huang’s on-clock CNS papers were hand-checked as genuinely his (none led); Bo Wang’s volume is not credible.

Dossier · Huang, Po-ssu undecided

At year four: 4.6 papers/yr — p30 of decided Engineering — but 6 on-clock CNS papers, p99.7. The most flagship-heavy undecided record in the department, none of it as senior author, and a clock in its tenth year.

At year six, among those still undecided at year six

On PC1 — the all-metrics size axis of chapter V — this record sits p78 of decided Engineering. Postscript, after the year-4 window (his works file stops at 2020): seven flagship-family items as last author since 2021, five with the corresponding flag — including three Nature Biotechnology items in 2024 (clock year 8) and Cell Systems 2025 — as OpenAlex records them, genre not adjudicated. The owned senior-author flagship record his year-4 window lacked arrived, in the family tier, in the clock’s final act. [live OpenAlex, post-window sweep (src/recheck_gaps.py), checked 2026-08-28] Big-moment boxes by year four (chapter V): ✗ led CNS · ✗ top-decile led paper · ✗ R01-eq/CAREER as PI. As PI (NIH RePORTER): 1 project (R01; 1 as contact PI), $1.54M obligated to date — none of it by clock year four; the first award began in clock year 6. No NSF award as PI.

Dossier · Skylar-Scott, Mark undecided

At year four: 2.8 papers/yr, p15 of decided Engineering, 0 on-clock CNS papers (p41). The clock runs to 2028; by the base rates of chapter VIII, the modal outcome of any running clock is tenure.

At year six, among those still undecided at year six

On PC1 — the all-metrics size axis of chapter V — this record sits p44 of decided Engineering. Postscript, after the year-4 window: "Rapid model-guided design of organ-scale synthetic vasculature for biomanufacturing," Science, June 2025 (clock year 5) — Skylar-Scott co-corresponding (Sexton first author, Marsden co-corresponding). At year four this existed only as an arXiv preprint, middle-author, which the primary counts correctly exclude; the published version checks the led-CNS box — the heaviest independent factor in the big-moment model — one year after the window every table on this page measures. His 2022 Nature Biomedical Engineering paper (first author; the publisher’s corresponding flag is a metadata error, hand-corrected in data/authorship_patches.json) sits in the family tier, which is why the strict three-title register read zero at year four. [live OpenAlex, W4386271217, checked 2026-08-28] Big-moment boxes by year four (chapter V): ✗ led CNS · ✗ top-decile led paper · ✓ R01-eq/CAREER as PI. As PI (NIH RePORTER): 4 projects (DP2, R01, R21, UM1; 2 as contact PI), $6.85M obligated to date — $2.05M of it by clock year four; the first award began in clock year 2. No NSF award as PI.

The as-PI lines cover federal money the public APIs can see: NIH RePORTER and the NSF awards register, nothing else. DARPA, DOE, VA and foundation support — which all three fields lean on — is invisible here, so a $0 is a floor, not a bank balance. And acknowledged funding on papers is not the same fact: ECCS-2026822, acknowledged on Skylar-Scott’s papers, is the nano@stanford shared-facility grant, PI Senesky. Source: src/pi_grants.py → data/pi_grants.json.

A promotion case is voted in the department but survives or dies against the school’s standard — the level where every recent case in the school is the yardstick. So here is that yardstick: every decided Engineering leaver at year four, ranked on the combined axis, with the live Bioengineering clocks slotted in. The leaver median sits at PC1 -0.60 against the tenured +0.20. Po-ssu Huang (+0.53) out-ranks 25 of the 26 leavers — p96 of the leaver distribution, above the tenured median — and holds more acknowledged funders than any of them. Paul Nuyujukian (-0.33) and Mark Skylar-Scott (-0.14) sit between the two medians. One caution the table itself supplies: the top of Engineering’s leaver list is a recruiting ledger — Washington, Berkeley, Harvard, MIT twice — so in this school “resembles the leavers” does not mean “resembles the denied.” Engineering’s strong records leave too; they leave upward.

VIII

How I Learned to Stop Worrying

The machine is real, and it is weaker than everyone believes.

Every AUC on this page sits near 0.70, which sounds decisive and is not: it means a randomly drawn future-tenured record out-ranks a randomly drawn future-leaver seven times in ten — and three times in ten it does not. The decided base rate is 70% tenured. A record in the bottom fifth of its own field’s rate at year four still reached tenure 63% of the time; the top fifth, 89%. Nothing in this battery — not the rate, not a Nature paper, not an NIH grant line, not the principal component of all of them together — predicts an individual case. The clock measures populations. People are decided one at a time, by committees reading letters this data never sees.

And one asymmetry is worth carrying out of the war room: “left” is not “denied.” A quarter of the leavers surface at Berkeley, Princeton, Harvard, MIT. The minutes cannot tell a denial from a better offer — though the thinness of the average leaver’s record leans one way — and the population that stays undecided longest is the one nobody should read anything into at all. That is how you stop worrying: the doomsday device is real, its yield is a coin flip with a thumb on it, and the thumb is the publication count.

Rechecks — hunting the Skylar-Scott class of gap

One case showed how a point-in-time snapshot can lag reality: a window-era preprint whose journal version — with a corresponding flag — published after the window. Three corpus-wide sweeps followed (src/recheck_corr.py, src/recheck_gaps.py; logs in results/). Stale corresponding flags: all 349 on-clock CNS papers stored as non-corresponding were re-fetched live — zero flags changed; the register is current. Missed journal versions: 5,867 on-clock preprints have no same-title article among the person’s works; a random 29 audited live found 2 whose article did exist by the anchor (7%% of the exposed class, ≈0.6%% of all works) — a small undercount, neither case a flagship, no sign it favors either arm. Post-window events: the live clocks’ works stop at year 4 by design; everything they published since was swept live and recorded as dated dossier postscripts, never folded into the year-4 tables.

Caveats that travel with every chapter: OpenAlex misses books and humanities output; the corresponding-author flag exists on only 21–28% of papers; funding metadata is a floor, not an inventory; two Bioengineering records carry merged-identity contamination and are flagged where shown; censored means undecided, and undecided means undecided.
